questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a negative psychotic symptom?

options.text: Flat affect
Apathy
Disorganized thinking
Avolition
Poverty of thought

questions.explanation: Positive psychotic symptoms consist of hallucinations, delusions, and bizarre or disorganized thinking and behavior[cite: 10]. Negative psychotic symptoms consist of flat affect, apathy, avolition (difficulty making choices), poverty of speech, and poverty of thought content[cite: 10]. Youth with schizophrenia, similar to adults with the disorder, are required to demonstrate positive or negative symptoms for at least 6 months and to have significant social or occupational dysfunction or failure to achieve expected levels of social development[cite: 10]. In addition, although not yet formally part of the fourth edition revised text version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV-TR) criteria, schizophrenia is associated with marked neurocognitive declines in general cognition, executive functioning, social cognition, and memory[cite: 10]. Indeed, these symptoms, not positive symptoms, seem most closely related to long-term functional outcome[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: Predictors of poor prognosis in schizophrenia with childhood onset include all of the following except

options.text: onset before 10 years of age
premorbid diagnoses of ADHD and learning disorders
lack of family support
delayed motor milestones and delayed language acquisition
misdiagnosed schizophrenia in a child with bipolar I disorder

correct_answer.text: misdiagnosed schizophrenia in a child with bipolar I disorder

correct_answers.text: misdiagnosed schizophrenia in a child with bipolar I disorder

questions.explanation: In children with bipolar I disorder, mania with psychotic features, with no prior history of depressive episodes, may be mistaken for schizophrenia; the distinction is crucial because bipolar I disorder has a better prognosis than schizophrenia in children[cite: 10]. Factors that appear to be related to poor prognosis in childhood schizophrenia include onset before 10 years of age; premorbid ADHD and learning disorders; lack of family support; and developmental delays, including delays in acquiring motor milestones and language[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is helpful in distinguishing COS from autistic disorder?

options.text: Intelligence
Family history of schizophrenia
Age of onset of symptoms
Presence of formal thought disorder
All of the above

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia with childhood onset can be differentiated from autistic disorder based on a number of key diagnostic and epidemiological features[cite: 10]. The age of onset distinguishes the two[cite: 10]. Whereas autistic children must display delays or abnormal functioning before age 3 years, schizophrenia is considered not to present before age 5 years[cite: 10]. Intelligence is another factor to consider; autistic children most often have impaired intelligence, but COS is usually associated with normal-range IQ[cite: 10]. The presence of a formal thought disorder is one of several core symptoms of schizophrenia but is not characteristic of autistic disorder[cite: 10]. Family history of schizophrenia is an important risk factor for COS but has not been shown to contribute to the risk for autistic disorder[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: All of the following statements regarding hallucinations in prepubertal children are true except

options.text: Auditory and visual hallucinations occur commonly in childhood-onset schizophrenia.
Childhood-onset schizophrenia cannot be diagnosed in the absence of hallucinations.
Visual hallucinations are not common in childhood schizophrenia.
Auditory hallucinations may occur in children exposed to extreme stress.
Auditory hallucinations occur in childhood mood disorders.

correct_answer.text: Childhood-onset schizophrenia cannot be diagnosed in the absence of hallucinations.

correct_answers.text: Childhood-onset schizophrenia cannot be diagnosed in the absence of hallucinations.

questions.explanation: Childhood-onset schizophrenia can be diagnosed in the absence of hallucinations; patients must have at least two of the following symptoms: hallucinations, delusions, grossly disorganized speech or behavior, and severe social withdrawal[cite: 10]. These symptoms must cause a disturbance in the child’s functioning characterized by deterioration in function or failure to achieve developmental milestones lasting at least 6 months[cite: 10]. Auditory hallucinations commonly occur in children with schizophrenia, and their content may be characterized by ongoing critical commentary or commands[cite: 10]. Visual hallucinations are also commonly experienced by children with schizophrenia and often have frightening content[cite: 10]. Hallucinations, particularly auditory hallucinations, commonly occur in children with mood disorders; these tend to be mood-congruent and tend to be less bizarre than hallucinations occurring in children with schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Both auditory and visual hallucinations may occur in children exposed to extreme stress and do not necessarily indicate the presence of a psychotic or mood disorder[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: Patients with which illness are most likely to have chromosomal abnormalities or mutations involving genes in neurodevelopmental pathways?

options.text: Adult-onset schizophrenia
Early-onset bipolar disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Adult-onset bipolar disorder
Early-onset schizophrenia

questions.explanation: Individuals with early-onset schizophrenia are significantly more likely than those with adult-onset schizophrenia to have chromosomal abnormalities or mutations involving genes in neurodevelopmental pathways[cite: 10]. Genetic vulnerabilities also appear more prominent in those with early-onset schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Youth with early-onset schizophrenia are at least twice as likely as individuals with adult-onset schizophrenia to have a parent with the disorder, and the morbid risk of schizophrenia for parents of individuals with early-onset schizophrenia ranges from 14 to 25 percent[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding COS is true?

options.text: Command hallucinations do not occur among children with schizophrenia.
Patients with COS are usually mildly to moderately mentally retarded.
Rates of schizophrenia are less common among parents of patients with COS than among parents of patients with adult-onset schizophrenia.
Among children with schizophrenia, there is often a premorbid history of behavioral disturbances, delayed motor milestones, and delayed language acquisition.
Symptoms of childhood schizophrenia respond more robustly to antipsychotic medication than do symptoms of adult-onset schizophrenia.

correct_answer.text: Among children with schizophrenia, there is often a premorbid history of behavioral disturbances, delayed motor milestones, and delayed language acquisition.

correct_answers.text: Among children with schizophrenia, there is often a premorbid history of behavioral disturbances, delayed motor milestones, and delayed language acquisition.

questions.explanation: Children diagnosed with schizophrenia commonly have a history of premorbid behavioral disturbances, delayed motor milestones, and delayed language acquisition[cite: 10]. Command auditory hallucinations, as well as other types of auditory hallucinations and visual hallucinations, commonly occur in children with schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Rates of schizophrenia are more common (not less common) among parents of patients with COS compared with parents of patients with adult-onset schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Although antipsychotic medications, particularly second-generation or atypical antipsychotics, are indicated for the treatment of patients with COS, symptoms in these patients tend to respond less robustly (not more robustly) to these medications than among patients with adult-onset schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Epidemiological data indicate that patients with COS are usually not (rather than mildly to moderately) mentally retarded but rather function in the low-average to average range of intelligence[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: All of the following are true statements about the course and prognosis of depression in children and adolescents except

options.text: early onset predicts a poorer prognosis.
depressive disorders are associated with long-term peer relationship difficulties.
risk of suicide is significant among adolescents with major depressive disorder.
short-term complications include poor academic achievement.
there is no increased risk of later developing bipolar disorder among adolescents with a major depressive episode compared with nondepressed teens.

correct_answer.text: there is no increased risk of later developing bipolar disorder among adolescents with a major depressive episode compared with nondepressed teens.

correct_answers.text: there is no increased risk of later developing bipolar disorder among adolescents with a major depressive episode compared with nondepressed teens.

questions.explanation: Several factors are known to worsen the prognosis of depression in children and adolescents, including early onset, multiple recurrent episodes, family history of significantly impairing depressive illness, and living in families with sustained and severe interpersonal conflict[cite: 10]. Depressive disorders are associated with short- and long-term peer relationship difficulties, poor academic achievement, and low self-esteem; additionally, there is a well-established increase in risk of suicide among adolescents with major depression[cite: 10]. Adolescents who have a major depressive episode are at significantly increased risk of going on to develop bipolar disorder compared with nondepressed teens[cite: 10].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding velocardiofacial syndrome (VCFS) is false?

options.text: Approximately 25 percent of patients with VCFS become psychotic in adolescence.
Approximately 5 percent of people with schizophrenia may have VCFS.
The incidence of VCFS is approximately one in 4,000 live births.
Individuals with VCFS frequently have mild mental retardation.
Individuals with VCFS commonly have a history of feeding problems in infancy.

correct_answer.text: Approximately 5 percent of people with schizophrenia may have VCFS.

correct_answers.text: Approximately 5 percent of people with schizophrenia may have VCFS.

questions.explanation: There is a high reported prevalence of genetic abnormalities in early-onset schizophrenia[cite: 10]. One abnormality is chromosome 22q11 deletion syndrome or velocardiofacial syndrome (VCFS)[cite: 10]. Approximately 25 percent of individuals with VCFS become psychotic during adolescence, with most experiencing schizophrenia[cite: 10]. Because the incidence of VCFS is estimated at one in 4,000 live births, as many as 10 percent (not 5 percent) of individuals with schizophrenia may have VCFS (see Figure 50.1 on p. 374)[cite: 10]. Frequently, individuals with VCFS have low facial tone, small mouths, learning disabilities, or mild mental retardation and a variety of congenital malformations, especially of the heart and palate[cite: 10]. A history of feeding problems in infancy is common[cite: 10].
